newsitem.title: UK: Greycoat says will defeat break-up attempts.
newsitem.headline: Greycoat says will defeat break-up attempts.

text.p: British property company Greycoat Plc said on Monday it expected dissident shareholders to fail again in their attempt to force the firm to liquidate its 500 million stg portfolio.
Chief executive Peter Thornton told Reuters in an interview the company currently had no plans to sell its property holdings, which are clustered in central London.
"From our point of view, it's an unwelcome and costly distraction," he said.

"It doesn't make any sense at all to sell off a portfolio in a market that is rising. We've got a good development programme currently under way. It's far too premature to consider selling," Thornton said.
Earlier, investment funds controlling an 11 percent stake in the company requested an extraordinary shareholders meeting to try to push the company to sell off its holdings.

"Having spoken to a number of shareholders, we believe that there is considerable support for our proposal, which will enhance shareholder value," said Bryan Myerson of Active Value Advisors Ltd, which advises the funds.
But the dissident funds, including UK Active Value Fund, IMP UKAV Inc and Chaddesley Investments, said a controlled disposal programme would enhance shareholder value significantly.
"The shares stand at a 23 percent discount to forecast 1997 net asset value, despite the fact that Greycoat has a high-quality portfolio," Myerson said in a statement on Sunday.
Thornton attributed the company's high discount in part to the funds' efforts to force a portfolio sale.
"It can't be attractive to other shareholders to know that this block (of shares) is sitting around waiting to be sold at some stage," he said.
But Thornton noted that a similar attempt by the funds earlier this year was unsuccessful. "I would doubt that Myerson has considerable support," he said.
Property analysts also voiced their doubts.
"I personally think this will fail," one analyst said. "The same people raised the same sort of questions a while back, and it didn't amount to much."
An analyst at SBC Warburg agreed, noting that Greycoat had active management and a strong development programme.
"I'm not aware that there is a huge amount of criticism about what Greycoat are doing," he said.
Analysts said the company's recent stock buyback programme for up to five percent of its shares reflected the company's awareness of its above-average discount.

"The company is in a position to buy back more shares if it wants to. The problem with that, of course is that every time they buy in shares, they're increasing Mr. Myerson's percentage holding," the SBC Warburg analyst said.
Thornton said Greycoat planned to continue with its current strategy, which includes completing the development of two office properties in just over 12 months' time and a third within 18 months.
"We're going to demonstrate that what we're doing will add to shareholder value and that what is proposed (by Myerson) will be disaster," he said.
